title: You speak more Spanish than you think

entries.note: A historic Spanish borrowing for a fleet of ships, famously the Spanish Armada, meaning an armed force; etymologically the Spanish equivalent of [[same-root:army]].
Spanish for little armoured one, formed by adding a diminutive to the root of [[same-root:armada]].
Came into English from French and is etymologically the same as [[same-root:armada]].
The Spanish word for war is Germanic rather than Latin, left by the [[see:Franks]], sharing its roots with French [[same-root:guerre]] and English [[same-root:war]].
Means little war, from [[from:guerra]]; entered English during the [[see:Peninsular War]] for ad hoc bands of Spanish peasants fighting alongside regular forces.
War of 1808 to 1814, stirred up by [[see:Napoleon]], during which [[see:guerrilla]] and [[see:junta]] entered English.
Sometimes pronounced with a J in English, it named the regional controlling councils and took off during the [[see:Peninsular War]].
Ultimately the reason English got [[see:guerrilla]] and [[see:junta]], since he stirred up the [[see:Peninsular War]].
Like English [[same-root:war]], a Germanic word with the same roots as Spanish [[same-root:guerra]].
Germanic word sharing its roots with French [[same-root:guerre]] and Spanish [[same-root:guerra]].
The source of Germanic words like [[see:guerra]] that are found in Romance languages.
An anglicisation of [[from:Jerez de la Frontera]], first used for that region's white wine and now for its fortified wine.
The Spanish wine region, now called Jerez de la Frontera, whose name gave [[gave:sherry]], though written down it looks little like it.
From Spanish [[from:alcorque]], an Iberian and North African oak spread through Europe in the 1300s; the root is Latin [[from:quercus]], oak.
Originally a word for bark, and said to be related to Latin [[same-root:quercus]], the root of [[same-root:cork]].
An afternoon nap, from Latin [[from:sexta]], sixth, because it was traditionally taken at the sixth hour of the day, around midday.
From the Latin for nine, as the ninth hour of the day (about 3 pm), but it came to mean midday; a story similar to [[see:siesta]].
Someone with affection for something, first used of amateur bullfighters or bullfighting fans; directly related to [[same-root:affection]] and comparable to [[see:amateur]].
Literally means someone who does something for the love of it rather than for money, just like [[see:aficionado]].
Directly related to [[same-root:aficionado]].
The Spanish word for olive oil comes from Arabic and, like many Arabic loans, keeps the Arabic definite article al- at the front.
Via Spanish, probably from a Quechua word like [[from?:paqo]], yellowish red, the animal's usual coat colour; al- was added on the mistaken assumption it was Arabic.
From Greek [[from:amygdalos]], with al- added in Spanish on the assumption that it was Arabic, like [[see:alpaca]].
Changed in English from [[from:alcatraz]], perhaps under the influence of Latin [[see:alba]], white; the reverse of what happened with [[see:alpaca]].
Iberian Spanish word for a pelican, from Arabic [[from?:al-qadus]], the jar (the pouch), or possibly [[from?:al-ghattas]], the diver; it gave [[gave:albatross]].
Came into English from Spanish but ultimately comes from Arabic.
Came via Spanish from an Arabic word for a dome or vault.
From Spanish [[from:el lagarto]], the lizard, originally lagarto de Indias, lizard of the Indies; the al- is not Arabic.
Related to Spanish lagarto, the source of [[same-root:alligator]], but took a different route into English.
An old English adjective for muscly, because muscles supposedly looked like lizards crawling under the skin; compare [[see:muscle]].
Means mousy, as if mice were crawling under the skin, an image like that behind [[see:lacertous]].
Via Spanish from the Taíno (Arawakan) name for the animal; [[see:Charles Darwin]] was rude about Galápagos marine iguanas.
A nickname for the [[see:iguana]], for its flavour and high protein; compared to calling pigeons [[see:rats of the skies]].
A nickname for pigeons that Rob compares with the iguana's nickname [[see:pollo de los árboles]].
Called Galápagos [[see:iguana]]s hideous, stupid and sluggish but skilful swimmers, and reportedly kept throwing one into the sea to see if it came back.
Mocked by Europeans who ate the bird to extinction; the name is a Portuguese take on another word and may mean stupid person.
Home of the [[see:dodo]]; it had no native population, which makes the bird's name hard to pin down.
From Spanish, used in the slave trade for someone who spoke Spanish poorly or seemed less intelligent; vaudeville turned it into a clown name.
Said to come from Spanish via the same slave-trade context and to mean a person on a small galley; now a big, awkward, clumsy person.
From Nahuatl [[from:coyotl]], an animal and a trickster god; Spanish added the final T, and English took it up by the early 1800s, replacing [[see:prairie wolf]].
The earlier English name for the [[see:coyote]], though coyotes share only about 4% of their genes with wolves.
Another case, like [[see:prairie wolf]], of naming an unfamiliar animal after one from home.
Like [[see:coyote]], a Nahuatl word ending in a tl sound that Spanish speakers in Mexico changed to end in -te.
A Nahuatl word taken up by Spanish colonists, which dropped its ending; it first meant [[see:jaguar]]s but English applied it to the smaller spotted cat.
Came from Portuguese, which took it from the Tupi-Guarani languages spoken in [[see:Brazil]].
Speaks Portuguese because it sticks across the Spanish–Portuguese dividing line, the original [[see:demarcation]] line; it has the most Portuguese speakers in the world.
Means pregnant in Spanish, a false friend of Portuguese [[same-root:embaraçada]] (embarrassed) and of English embarrassed.
Means embarrassed in Portuguese, a false friend of Spanish [[same-root:embarazada]], pregnant.
Means exquisite in Spanish, whereas Portuguese [[same-root:esquisito]] means strange, a shift compared with [[see:peculiar]].
Means strange in Portuguese, a false friend of Spanish [[same-root:exquisito]], exquisite.
Can mean both special and weird, showing how [[see:exquisito]] and [[see:esquisito]] diverged; closely related to [[same-root:particular]].
Closely related to [[same-root:peculiar]].
Means drinking glass in Spanish, while Portuguese [[same-root:vaso]] can mean vase or toilet bowl.
A name for the th sound of Spain, explained by a false story about copying a lisping [[see:King Ferdinand]]; actually it is a distinct sound, see [[see:distinción]].
The king said in a nonsense story to have had a lisp that Spaniards copied, giving the [[see:Spanish lisp]].
Pronunciation mostly used in Spain, which separates an s sound from a th sound, so [[see:caza]] and [[see:casa]] differ; contrasted with [[see:seseo]] and [[see:ceceo]].
Latin American pronunciation with no th sound, brought by emigrants from [[see:Andalusia]] and the Canaries, making [[see:caza]] and [[see:casa]] homophones.
Pronunciation found in parts of [[see:Andalusia]] where even a normal s is said as th, as in gracias.
Distinct from [[see:casa]] in Castilian [[see:distinción]] but pronounced the same with Latin American [[see:seseo]].
A homophone of [[see:caza]] in Latin America, but not in Spain.
The name for Iberian Spanish, which uses [[see:distinción]].
Home of most Spaniards who crossed the Atlantic, which is why its [[see:seseo]] travelled to Latin America.
Jess's emblematic example of [[see:distinción]], said with a th sound in Castilian Spanish.
Used much more widely in Latin America than in Spain and is the safest second-person pronoun there, where [[see:tú]] can seem over-informal.
The informal you, more common in Spain; in Latin America it can seem over-familiar or rude with people who aren't close, unlike [[see:usted]].
Spain's informal plural you, all but lost in Latin America, which uses [[see:ustedes]] instead.
The plural you that Latin America uses instead of [[see:vosotros]].
Linda or lindo, beautiful, is the more Latin American choice; Spain prefers [[see:guapa]].
Guapa or guapo, handsome or beautiful, is more common in Spain, where Latin America says [[see:linda]].
From Spanish [[from:vaquero]], cowboy, where v and b sound alike; related to French [[same-root:vache]] and cow words like [[same-root:vaccination]].
Related to vaquero, the source of [[same-root:buckaroo]].
One of the cow-related words connected to [[same-root:buckaroo]].
From Spanish [[from:mesteño]], stray animal, named after the [[from:Honrado Concejo de la Mesta]]; a wild horse isn't called a mustang outside the Americas.
A 14th-century Spanish livestock owners' association whose annual assemblies divided up strays; mesta supposedly comes from Latin for mixed. It gave [[gave:mustang]].
Spanish for untamed, as in caballo bronco, untamed horse; English took just the bronco part to mean an untamed horse.
Common in mountain range names, it means saw because the ranges are jagged; related to [[same-root:serrated]].
Related to [[same-root:sierra]], saw.
The same word as [[same-root:cannon]], meaning tube; the English Y spells out the sound of Spanish cañón's [[see:eñe]].
The same word as [[same-root:cañón]], both meaning tube.
The letter ñ began as a double N; scribes put one N above the other, which shrank to a squiggle, as in [[see:año]].
Once written with a double N, it now uses the [[see:eñe]].
The squiggle on the [[see:eñe]], from Latin [[from:titulus]], heading or superscription; related to [[same-root:title]] and, by [[see:metathesis]], to [[same-root:tittle]].
Shares its Latin origin, titulus, with [[same-root:tilde]].
The dot on an I or J, also from Latin titulus like [[same-root:tilde]].
One of the hosts' favourite things, seen in the difference between [[see:tilde]] and [[see:tittle]].
Originally meant an enclosure, a place where things were rounded up; related to [[same-root:round]].
Related to [[same-root:rodeo]].
From Spanish [[from:lazo]], string or cord, with a th in Castilian; British English oddly says lassoo. Directly related to [[same-root:lace]].
Directly related to [[same-root:lasso]], since lace is a material made of string and cord.
Means pine cone and is used for pineapples in peninsular Spanish, as in [[see:piña colada]]; many other Spanish speakers say [[see:ananas]]. Shares its origin with [[same-root:piñata]].
From Latin [[from:pinea]], pine cone; in Mexican Spanish it meant a jug or pot, probably because of its shape.
First meant a pine cone; in the 1660s English and Spanish speakers in the Caribbean applied it to the fruit, which looked like big pine cones. Compare [[see:piña]].
What most of the world calls the [[see:pineapple]], used by many Spanish speakers instead of [[see:piña]].
A drink whose name uses [[see:piña]] for pineapple.
A frontier word from Spanish for good weather or prosperity, from Latin bonus, which also gave [[same-root:bonus]].
From the same Latin word as [[same-root:bonanza]]; the opposite of French [[see:malus]].
Used in French sports scoring for points deducted, the opposite of a [[see:bonus]]; Rob thinks English should adopt it.
Adopted in 1737 from Spanish línea de demarcación, the line [[see:Pope Alexander VI]] drew in 1493 to divide the New World between Spain and Portugal.
Laid down the original line of [[see:demarcation]] on 4 May 1493.
Means sauce, ultimately salted, and named a dance in the 1970s, presumably because it's saucy and spicy; related to [[same-root:salary]], [[same-root:salad]] and [[same-root:sauce]].
Goes back to salt, perhaps from being paid in salt, and is related to [[same-root:salsa]].
Originally meant something salted, like salted meats; related to [[same-root:salsa]] and [[same-root:sauce]].
Related to [[same-root:salsa]] and [[same-root:salad]] through salt.
Means flame-coloured in Spanish and Portuguese, from [[from:flamma]], flame; it's unclear whether it's related to [[same-root?:flamenco]].
Also meant a person from Flanders, equivalent to [[same-root:Flemish]]; perhaps because Spaniards conflated Flemish and Romani people or used Flemish for any foreigner.
The equivalent of [[same-root:flamenco]], which once also meant a person from Flanders, a place Spain controlled.
Given as an example of travellers being named after a distant place, as with [[see:gypsy]] and possibly [[see:flamenco]].
Essentially means people from Egypt, a case of naming travellers after a distant place, like [[see:flamenco]].
From Argentinian Spanish, originally the name of an African South American drum dance.
Cuban Spanish for party or spree; its further etymology is uncertain, though it may be related to [[same-root?:rhombus]].
Possibly related to [[same-root?:rumba]].
Came via Spanish from Haitian Creole, where, per the OED, it was a voodoo ritual dance or voodoo priestess.
The island shared by French-speaking Haiti and Spanish-speaking Dominican Republic, mentioned in the story of [[see:mambo]].
A dance name from Haitian and Dominican Creole meaning a mixture, related to [[same-root:meringue]]; Rob wonders whether [[see:melon]] is connected.
The sweet dessert, related to [[same-root:merengue]].
Rob speculates that it could be related to [[same-root?:merengue]] through an R and L swap.
